title: About Juan Lopez — Behavior Analyst
description: Juan Lopez is a behavior analyst, researcher, and digital systems designer working across care, research, websites, commerce, and data.
html:
About

Behavior Analyst, Researcher and Digital Systems Designer.

Juan Lopez studies how environments, information, and experiences affect people, then carries that understanding into clearer, more humane systems.

A shared foundation

Observation and implementation belong together.

Behavior analysis is the primary lens through which I approach my work. It brings careful observation, consistent measurement, individual context, and socially meaningful outcomes into the same conversation. Rather than beginning with assumptions, I try to understand the conditions surrounding a person, a task, or a system before deciding what should change.

My work in research, web development, e-commerce, and information design grows from that foundation. I build client websites with SitePad and WordPress, develop Shopify themes, and use Astro to create focused, lightweight websites. By shaping environments so that information is clearer, actions are easier to understand, and systems better support the people who use them.

Across independent client projects, I have managed the full path from early strategy to launch. My work has included information architecture, visual design, development, responsive implementation, content structure, forms, business email, payment systems, and domain configuration. Each part of that process is guided by the same goal: create something practical without losing sight of the person on the other side of the screen.

I am completing two bachelor’s degrees at Florida International University: Psychology on the Applied Behavior Analysis track, and Natural and Applied Sciences. My current credentials include Registered Behavior Technician certification through the Behavior Analyst Certification Board and Social and Behavioral Human Research training through the CITI Program. I also hold certifications in food safety management and agricultural studies, reflecting a broader foundation in responsible practice, applied science, and human-centered work.

Research

Questions designed to be tested

I designed my Fall 2025 AI Misattribution study to examine how expectations about a source shape social evaluation. Using an online experiment, Qualtrics, and IBM SPSS, I kept the question focused, the conditions controlled, and the conclusions grounded in what the data could support.

Client systems

From early structure to launch

I build websites for service businesses using SitePad, WordPress, and Astro, depending on what the project requires. My work can include information structure, responsive design, forms, business email, payments, domain configuration, content organization, and the final details needed to bring a complete website online.

Commerce

Storefronts with a clear direction

Through World Cup Items and VX Nexus, I have developed Shopify themes, shaped visual direction, organized merchandising, configured commerce systems, and refined each storefront across screen sizes. I approach e-commerce as an environment that should make products easier to understand, compare, and act on without adding unnecessary pressure.

Real-world experience

Understanding people in motion.

Working as a valet attendant has placed me in environments where trust, timing, communication, and attention matter immediately. Every shift requires me to observe what is happening, respond to changing conditions, and help people move through an experience with less uncertainty.

  • Observation
  • Coordination
  • Responsibility
  • Adaptation
Live environment In motion
  1. 01 Arrival Read the entrance
  2. 02 Handoff Establish trust
  3. 03 Coordinate Adapt with the team
  4. 04 Return Complete the experience
01

Observation

Reading the environment

A busy entrance changes from one moment to the next. I pay attention to traffic, guest behavior, available space, team movement, and the small cues that signal what may be needed next. The work has taught me to look carefully before acting.

02

Trust

Responsibility made visible

People hand me something valuable and expect it to be handled with care. I build that trust through clear communication, consistency, attention to detail, and respect for each person’s circumstances.

03

Adaptation

Staying clear under pressure

Arrivals overlap, priorities shift, and unexpected problems appear quickly. I have learned to remain composed, coordinate with others, and adjust to changing conditions without losing sight of the person waiting in front of me.

A system is not defined only by how it works under ideal conditions, but by how well it supports people when time, attention, and patience are already limited.

Real conditions. Thoughtful responses.

title: Behavior Analysis–Informed Digital Design
description: A behavior-analytic, evidence-informed approach to research and digital systems grounded in clarity, dignity, autonomy, and meaningful outcomes.
html:
Approach

Evidence with humility. Structure with care.

I study how environments and information affect what people can understand and accomplish. The goal is not to control people. It is to remove avoidable barriers and make choices easier to see.

01

Everyday language first

Technical vocabulary is useful only when it makes the reasoning more precise. People should not need a glossary to understand the point.

02

Context matters

A pattern is interpreted alongside the environment, the task, and the individual—not as a detached number.

03

Meaningful outcomes

Measurement should return to what a person or team can do, understand, and choose in the real setting.

ABA-Informed Design Pathway

Five translations from research to practice.

Each step connects an everyday need to a restrained behavioral concept and a practical design implication.

  1. 01

    Stimulus salience and attending

    Make What Matters Easy to Notice

    Visual hierarchy, contrast, and placement make task-relevant information easier to distinguish from supporting detail. The most useful next action should stand out without competing unnecessarily for attention.

    Design implication: prioritize the next useful action, then layer in supporting detail.

  2. 02

    Discriminative stimuli

    Use Clear Cues for Action

    Labels, controls, and interface states should signal which actions are available and which are likely to work. Consistent cues reduce guesswork and help people move through a system with greater confidence.

    Design implication: use stable labels, recognizable controls, and predictable states.

  3. 03

    Task analysis, prompting, and fading

    Support Progress in Manageable Steps

    Complex tasks become more approachable when they are divided into meaningful steps and supported at the moment help is needed. That assistance should gradually recede as the person becomes more capable of completing the task independently.

    Design implication: sequence difficult tasks, provide timely guidance, and fade support when it is no longer needed.

  4. 04

    Consequences and reinforcement

    Make Outcomes Clear and Consistent

    Immediate, accurate feedback helps people determine whether an action worked. A consequence functions as reinforcement only when it makes the behavior it follows more likely to occur again.

    Design implication: confirm outcomes, preserve progress, and make effective actions easy to repeat.

  5. 05

    Social validity and data-based decisions

    Measure Meaningful Outcomes

    A useful system should be evaluated by outcomes that matter to the people using it. Measure whether important tasks become more successful, efficient, or independent, identify barriers, and revise the environment when results fall short.

    Design implication: define observable success with users and let the results guide refinement.

Ethical foundation

Autonomy and dignity are part of the method.

Behavior analysis is strongest when socially meaningful goals, informed choice, compassion, and respect are treated as requirements. In digital work, that means avoiding deceptive pressure, making outcomes understandable, and allowing people to change their minds.

Primary sources

  • Wolf (1978): social validity
  • Stimulus control research and practice
  • Prompting and fading research
  • BACB Ethics Code for Behavior Analysts
  • Baer, Wolf, and Risley: dimensions revisited

title: AI (Mis)attribution: Human–AI Research Study
description: An online experiment asking whether people judge the same interaction differently when they believe artificial intelligence is involved.
html:
Research · Fall 2025

AI (Mis)attribution

AI (Mis)attribution: Perceiver Expectations About Agent Origin as a Driver of Social Evaluations in Text-Based Interactions

Academic Research

Research question

Does the label change the judgment?

An online experiment asking whether people judge the same interaction differently when they believe artificial intelligence is involved.

QualtricsIBM SPSS Online study
Sample
N = 123
Conditions
Three
Transcript
Identical
Author
Juan D. Lopez
Course
FIU Research Methods II
Term
Fall 2025
Last reviewed
July 26, 2026
Administration
Online
Sample
N = 123 in Study One
Tools
Qualtrics and IBM SPSS
Methods
Online between-subjects experiment, Identical transcript control, Six-point evaluation scales
Conditions
Human–Human, Human–AI, AI–AI
Discuss the research

Short answer

What did the study find?

Participants rated the conversation as more natural when they believed both speakers were human, even though the transcript was unchanged.

This online course study was last reviewed on July 26, 2026. The interpretation and limitations below apply to this study's specific text-based setting.

Research question

Do people judge the same interaction differently when they believe artificial intelligence is involved?

Theoretical background

People interpret a message alongside beliefs about its source. Research on agency, social evaluation, and human–AI interaction suggests that labels can shape expectations before a conversation is evaluated.

Hypotheses

Study One predicted that origin labels would influence naturalness, humanness, and thoughtfulness ratings. The warm-versus-cold extension tested whether tone would alter evaluations differently for human-labeled and AI-labeled responses.

Study One design

The study was conducted online. One hundred twenty-three participants were assigned equally to Human–Human, Human–AI, or AI–AI conditions. Each person evaluated the same approximately 446-word transcript. Only the stated origin of the speakers changed.

Questionnaire and participant materials were created in Qualtrics. Data were analyzed in IBM SPSS.

Main finding

Naturalness differed across the three label conditions, F(2, 120) = 8.05, p < .001. The Human–Human condition received higher ratings than Human–AI and AI–AI. The two AI-involved labels did not differ significantly from each other.

This supports a bounded conclusion: in this study, the label surrounding the exchange affected how the unchanged conversation was evaluated.

Proposed and completed extension

The second study crossed responder identity with warm or cold tone. The strongest pattern was that warmth improved evaluations of a human-labeled response, while the same tone contrast did not change evaluations of an AI-labeled response in the same way.

Limitations

The research used convenience university samples and one text-based academic context. Those limits matter. The results should not be generalized to all people, all AI systems, or all forms of conversation.

Reflection

The study made context impossible to ignore. People were not only responding to words; they were responding to what they believed those words represented.

Method at a glance

The control was the conversation itself.

Held constant

  • The same approximately 446-word transcript
  • The online evaluation flow
  • The response scales

Changed

  • The stated origin of the two speakers
  • Human–Human, Human–AI, or AI–AI label

Available evidence

What can—and cannot—be claimed.

Available outcomes

  • Study One found higher naturalness ratings in the Human–Human condition than in either condition labeled as involving AI

Limitations

  • Convenience university sample
  • Single text-based academic interaction
  • Results should not be generalized to every AI interaction

Responsible interpretation

A difference in this setting, not a universal rule.

The findings show that origin beliefs affected social evaluation in the study's text-based context. They do not establish that all people reject AI, that labels always dominate content, or that any system can control judgment.

Juan can move from a question to a working system while keeping scope, evidence, access, and human consequences visible.

Data & Content Systems

Tools that organize information, reveal patterns, and support more informed decisions.

How projects are framed

Useful before impressive. Clear before clever.

An intervention and a project begin the same way: by clarifying who they are for and what meaningful change should look like. I use observation, interviews, and analytics to understand the context, identify barriers, and define clear standards for measuring success. From there, I build and refine solutions based on what the evidence shows, moving closer to outcomes that are practical, ethical, and meaningful to the people they are meant to support.

  1. Observe the real setting and context
  2. Define clear problem specifications
  3. Measure baseline behavior and data
  4. Analyze underlying patterns and barriers
  5. Test practical design interventions
  6. Refine from empirical evidence

No guaranteed conversions or predetermined human outcomes.

title: AI Misattribution Case Study
description: An online experiment testing whether labels about AI involvement change judgments of the same interaction.
html:
Research & Behavioral Systems

AI Misattribution

In Study One, 123 participants evaluated an identical transcript under three stated-origin conditions. Only the label changed.

Academic Research
Status
Academic Research
Role
Student researcher and author
Platform
Qualtrics and IBM SPSS · Confirmed
Project type
Academic research · Supplied by Juan
Timeframe
Fall 2025
Last reviewed
July 26, 2026

Date source: Course term confirmed by Juan.

The source paper was reviewed. Study One was conducted online, as clarified by Juan.

Context

The work in context.

The study asked whether expectations about who produced a conversation can influence social judgments even when the words are unchanged.

Case study summary

What did Juan build?

An online experiment testing whether labels about AI involvement change judgments of the same interaction.

This case study was last reviewed on July 26, 2026. Project details and limitations are identified throughout the page.

Role, audience and objectives

Responsibility carried through the system.

Juan's role

  • Research question and literature review
  • Experimental materials and questionnaire
  • Online study administration
  • Qualtrics implementation
  • IBM SPSS analysis
  • Interpretation and academic writing

Audience

  • Researchers studying human–AI interaction
  • Designers and teams communicating AI involvement

Objectives

  • Hold the transcript constant
  • Vary only the stated origin of the interaction
  • Measure perceived naturalness, humanness, and thoughtfulness

Behavioral lens

  • Context and expectations can affect evaluation
  • Measured outcomes should remain tied to the study conditions

Study One

One hundred twenty-three participants were assigned equally across three conditions: Human–Human, Human–AI, and AI–AI. Everyone read the same approximately 446-word transcript online. Only the stated origin changed.

Naturalness differed across conditions, F(2, 120) = 8.05, p < .001. Participants rated the Human–Human version more natural than either version described as involving AI. The Human–AI and AI–AI conditions did not differ significantly.

Study Two

The extension crossed responder identity with warm or cold tone. It asked whether tone changed evaluation in the same way for a response labeled human and a response labeled AI. The clearest pattern was that warmth improved ratings for the human-labeled response; it did not produce the same change for the AI-labeled response.

Interpretation

The findings support a careful conclusion: beliefs about origin can shape social evaluation in this text-based context. They do not show that people always reject AI, and they do not imply that labels control judgment.

Limitations

The studies used convenience university samples and a single academic interaction. Future work could test different relationships, settings, voices, avatars, and levels of perceived autonomy.

Information architecture and visual direction

Important structural decisions.

Information architecture

  • Consent and online questionnaire
  • Randomized label condition
  • Identical transcript
  • Six-point evaluation scales
  • SPSS analysis

Design decisions

  • Used an identical underlying transcript to isolate the label manipulation
  • Included Human–Human, Human–AI, and AI–AI conditions
  • Extended the work with a warm-versus-cold tone study

Technical implementation

Infrastructure, responsive behavior, and access.

Email, forms, payments and platform

  • Qualtrics questionnaire and participant materials
  • Online study administration
  • IBM SPSS data analysis

Accessibility and responsive design

  • Plain-language public summary
  • Labels written out before abbreviations
  • Findings described without implying determinism

Available evidence

What can—and cannot—be claimed.

Available outcomes

  • Study One found higher naturalness ratings in the Human–Human condition than in either condition labeled as involving AI

Limitations

  • Convenience university sample
  • Single text-based academic interaction
  • Results should not be generalized to every AI interaction

Reflection

What the project clarified.

The work reinforced that people do not evaluate language in a vacuum. The surrounding explanation can change how the same exchange is experienced.
